name: Letang v Cooper
subject: Torts
principle: Trespass to the person lies only for intentional direct acts; where the injury is caused unintentionally, the claim is in negligence and damage must be proved.
facts: The claimant was sunbathing in a hotel car park when the defendant drove over her legs. She sued more than three years later, framing the claim in trespass to escape the three-year limitation period that applied to negligence.
held: The claim failed. Lord Denning MR said that where the injury is inflicted intentionally the action is trespass, and where it is inflicted unintentionally the only action is negligence. Either way the claim was one for personal injuries and was time-barred.

name: Stephens v Myers
subject: Torts
principle: An assault requires an apparent present ability to carry out the threatened force; it is not necessary that the force is actually applied.
facts: At a parish meeting the defendant, angry, advanced on the chairman with a clenched fist, saying he would rather pull him out of the chair than be turned out of the room. He was stopped by others before he reached the chairman.
held: This was capable of being an assault. Advancing with intent to strike, within such distance that the blow would have landed but for the intervention, puts the claimant in apprehension of immediate force.

name: Tuberville v Savage
subject: Torts
principle: Words accompanying a threatening gesture can negate an assault where they show that no immediate violence is intended.
facts: The defendant laid his hand on his sword and said: 'If it were not assize-time, I would not take such language from you.'
held: No assault. The words showed that, because the assize judges were in town, he did not intend to use the sword, so there was no threat of immediate force.

name: Read v Coker
subject: Torts
principle: A conditional threat of immediate force, where the condition is one the defendant has no right to impose, can amount to assault.
facts: The claimant refused to leave the defendant's workshop. The defendant's workmen surrounded him, rolling up their sleeves and threatening to break his neck if he did not go. He left.
held: This was an assault. The threat of immediate violence was real, and the claimant left because of it.

name: Cole v Turner
subject: Torts
principle: The least touching of another in anger is a battery; touching without violence or intent to harm in ordinary situations is not.
facts: A short ruling of Holt CJ setting out when touching another person amounts to battery.
held: Holt CJ said the least touching of another in anger is a battery, but that people touching gently in a narrow passage, without violence or design of harm, commit no battery.

name: Collins v Wilcock
subject: Torts
principle: Any intentional touching beyond the physical contact generally acceptable in ordinary daily life is a battery, unless justified.
facts: A police officer, wanting to question a woman she suspected of soliciting but had no power to arrest, took hold of her arm to stop her walking away. The woman scratched the officer.
held: The officer had committed a battery, because holding the arm went beyond the everyday touching people impliedly accept, so the officer was not acting in the execution of her duty. Robert Goff LJ explained the 'exigencies of everyday life' exception.

name: R v Ireland
subject: Torts
principle: Words, and even silent telephone calls, can amount to an assault if they cause the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful force.
facts: The defendant made repeated silent telephone calls to three women, who suffered psychiatric illness as a result.
held: A silent call can be an assault if it causes fear of immediate violence, and recognised psychiatric illness can be bodily harm. Lord Steyn rejected the old view that words alone can never be an assault. (A criminal case, regularly cited on the meaning of assault in tort.)

name: Bird v Jones
subject: Torts
principle: False imprisonment requires a total restraint of movement; blocking one route while others remain open is not imprisonment.
facts: Part of a public bridge was fenced off for spectators of a boat race. The claimant tried to pass through the enclosure and was stopped, though he was free to go back and cross by the other side.
held: There was no false imprisonment. The restraint was partial, because he could go another way, and a prison must have boundaries on every side.

name: Meering v Grahame-White Aviation Co Ltd
subject: Torts
principle: A person can be falsely imprisoned without knowing it at the time.
facts: The claimant, suspected of theft, agreed to wait in a company office. Unknown to him, works police were posted outside to stop him leaving.
held: This was false imprisonment even though he did not know he was being detained. (Approved by the House of Lords in Murray v Ministry of Defence, which added that damages may then be nominal.)

name: Herd v Weardale Steel, Coal and Coke Co Ltd
subject: Torts
principle: There is no false imprisonment where a person has voluntarily entered a place on terms, and is held only until the agreed means of leaving is available.
facts: A miner went down the pit for his shift but then refused to work and asked to be brought up. The employer did not raise him until the end of the shift, about twenty minutes after the cage became available.
held: No false imprisonment. He had gone down on the terms of his employment, and the employer was not obliged to bring him up before the end of his shift.

name: Wilkinson v Downton
subject: Torts
principle: A person who wilfully does an act calculated to cause physical harm, including nervous shock, and causes it, is liable even without trespass.
facts: As a practical joke the defendant told the claimant that her husband had been badly injured in an accident. It was untrue, and she suffered a severe nervous shock and illness.
held: The defendant was liable. The statement was calculated to cause harm of this kind and did so. The case founded the tort of intentional infliction of harm.

name: Bradford Corporation v Pickles
subject: Torts
principle: Damnum sine injuria: harm caused by the lawful exercise of a right is not actionable, and a bad motive does not make a lawful act unlawful.
facts: Pickles sank shafts on his own land that cut off percolating water flowing to the corporation's reservoir, apparently to pressure the corporation into buying his land.
held: The corporation had no claim. Pickles was entitled to draw the water under his land, and his motive was irrelevant.

name: Donoghue v Stevenson
subject: Torts
principle: A person owes a duty of care to their 'neighbours' - those so closely and directly affected by their acts that they ought reasonably to have them in mind.
facts: Mrs Donoghue's friend bought her a bottle of ginger beer. The opaque bottle allegedly contained a decomposed snail, and she suffered shock and gastroenteritis. She had no contract with the manufacturer.
held: A manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer. Lord Atkin's neighbour principle became the foundation of the modern law of negligence.

name: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman
subject: Torts
principle: A duty of care requires foreseeability of damage, proximity between the parties, and that it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
facts: Investors relied on audited accounts to buy shares in a company and take it over. The accounts were inaccurate and the investors lost money.
held: The auditors owed no duty to investors. The accounts were prepared for shareholders as a body to oversee the company, not for people deciding whether to invest.

name: Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd
subject: Torts
principle: A duty of care for negligent statements causing pure economic loss can arise where there is a special relationship involving reliance and an assumption of responsibility.
facts: A bank gave a favourable credit reference about a customer to the claimants' bank, which relied on it. The customer went into liquidation and the claimants lost money. The reference said it was given 'without responsibility'.
held: Such a duty can exist, but the disclaimer prevented any duty arising on these facts, so the bank was not liable.

name: Bolton v Stone
subject: Torts
principle: A defendant is not negligent for failing to guard against a risk so small that a reasonable person would disregard it.
facts: A cricket ball was hit out of the ground and struck the claimant on a quiet road. Balls had left the ground only about six times in thirty years.
held: The club was not in breach of duty, because the risk of injury was so remote that a reasonable person would not have taken further precautions.

name: Nettleship v Weston
subject: Torts
principle: The standard of care is objective: a learner driver must meet the standard of a reasonably competent driver.
facts: A learner driver, being taught by a friend, hit a lamp post and the friend's knee was injured.
held: The learner was in breach of duty. Inexperience does not lower the standard of care owed.

name: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital Management Committee
subject: Torts
principle: Causation in fact: the claimant must show that, but for the defendant's breach, the harm would not have occurred.
facts: A man went to hospital after drinking tea and vomiting. The doctor on duty refused to examine him and sent him home. He died of arsenic poisoning.
held: The doctor was in breach of duty, but the hospital was not liable. The man would have died even with proper treatment, so the breach did not cause his death.

name: Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v Morts Dock & Engineering Co Ltd (The Wagon Mound No 1)
subject: Torts
principle: A defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable.
facts: Oil spilled from the defendants' ship into Sydney Harbour and spread to the claimants' wharf. Welding sparks ignited cotton waste floating in the oil, and the wharf was destroyed by fire.
held: The defendants were not liable for the fire damage, because it was not reasonably foreseeable that the oil would ignite on water. This replaced the 'direct consequence' test in Re Polemis.

name: Rylands v Fletcher
subject: Torts
principle: A person who brings onto their land something likely to do mischief if it escapes is liable for the damage its escape causes, if the use of the land is non-natural.
facts: The defendants had a reservoir built on their land. Water burst through old mine shafts that the contractors had not sealed and flooded the claimant's mine.
held: The defendants were liable without proof of negligence. The rule applies to non-natural uses of land.

name: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
subject: Contracts
principle: An advertisement can be a unilateral offer to the world, accepted by anyone who performs the stated conditions, without notifying acceptance.
facts: The company advertised that it would pay GBP 100 to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball as directed, and said it had deposited GBP 1,000 with a bank to show its sincerity. Mrs Carlill used the ball and caught influenza.
held: She was entitled to the GBP 100. The advertisement was an offer, not mere puffery, and performing the conditions was acceptance.

name: Fisher v Bell
subject: Contracts
principle: Displaying goods in a shop window with a price is an invitation to treat, not an offer.
facts: A shopkeeper displayed a flick knife in his window with a price ticket and was charged with 'offering it for sale', contrary to statute.
held: He was not guilty. In contract law the display was an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale.

name: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd
subject: Contracts
principle: Goods on self-service shelves are an invitation to treat; the customer makes the offer at the till, and the shop accepts there.
facts: Boots sold certain medicines from self-service shelves. The law required a pharmacist to supervise such sales, and one was present at the cash desk.
held: The sale took place at the cash desk, where the pharmacist was present, so there was no breach. The display was an invitation to treat.

name: Hyde v Wrench
subject: Contracts
principle: A counter-offer rejects the original offer, which cannot afterwards be accepted.
facts: Wrench offered to sell his farm for GBP 1,000. Hyde replied offering GBP 950, which was refused. Hyde then tried to accept the original GBP 1,000 offer.
held: There was no contract. The counter-offer had destroyed the original offer.

name: Adams v Lindsell
subject: Contracts
principle: The postal rule: where acceptance by post is contemplated, acceptance is complete when the letter is posted.
facts: The defendants offered to sell wool by a letter that was misdirected and arrived late. The claimants posted an acceptance the same day it arrived, but the defendants had already sold the wool to someone else.
held: A contract was formed when the acceptance was posted, so the defendants were in breach.

name: Entores Ltd v Miles Far East Corporation
subject: Contracts
principle: With instantaneous communication, acceptance takes effect when and where it is received by the offeror.
facts: An offer was made by telex from London to Amsterdam and accepted by telex from Amsterdam. The question was where the contract was made.
held: The contract was made in London, where the acceptance was received. The postal rule does not apply to instantaneous communications.

name: Currie v Misa
subject: Contracts
principle: Consideration is some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility suffered by the other.
facts: A dispute over whether a bill of exchange given to satisfy an existing debt was given for value.
held: The case is remembered for Lush J's classic definition of consideration in terms of benefit and detriment.

name: Stilk v Myrick
subject: Contracts
principle: Performing an existing contractual duty owed to the promisor is not good consideration for a promise of extra payment.
facts: Two sailors deserted a voyage. The captain promised the remaining crew the deserters' wages if they sailed the ship home, then refused to pay.
held: The crew could not recover the extra pay. They were already bound to sail the ship home, so they gave no consideration.

name: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd
subject: Contracts
principle: A promise to pay more for the performance of an existing duty can be enforceable if the promisor obtains a practical benefit and there is no duress or fraud.
facts: Main contractors promised a carpentry subcontractor extra money to finish work on time, because they faced a penalty clause if the work was late.
held: The promise was enforceable. Avoiding the penalty and the trouble of finding a replacement was a practical benefit that counted as consideration. This refined Stilk v Myrick.

name: Central London Property Trust Ltd v High Trees House Ltd
subject: Contracts
principle: Promissory estoppel: a clear promise not to enforce strict legal rights, intended to be acted on and acted on, binds the promisor even without consideration.
facts: During the war a landlord agreed to halve the rent of a block of flats because many were empty. After the war the landlord sought the full rent.
held: Full rent was payable from when the flats filled up again in 1945, but Denning J said the landlord would have been estopped from claiming full rent for the war years.

name: Foakes v Beer
subject: Contracts
principle: Part payment of a debt is not good consideration for a promise to forgo the balance.
facts: Mrs Beer agreed to let Dr Foakes pay a judgment debt in instalments, and later claimed the interest on the debt.
held: She was entitled to the interest. Paying part of what was already owed gave no consideration for her promise to forgo the rest.

name: Tweddle v Atkinson
subject: Contracts
topics: consideration must move from the promisee
principle: A person who is not a party to a contract cannot sue on it, even if it was made for their benefit.
facts: The fathers of a couple agreed with each other to pay the husband sums of money. The bride's father died without paying, and the husband sued his estate.
held: The husband could not sue. He was not a party to the agreement and had given no consideration for it.

name: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v Selfridge & Co Ltd
subject: Contracts
principle: Only a party to a contract who has given consideration can enforce it.
facts: Dunlop sold tyres to a dealer, who agreed not to sell below list price and to obtain the same promise from retailers. Selfridge bought from the dealer, made that promise to the dealer, then sold below list price.
held: Dunlop could not enforce Selfridge's promise. Dunlop was not a party to that contract and gave no consideration for it. Lord Haldane set out privity and consideration as fundamental principles.

name: Beswick v Beswick
subject: Contracts
principle: A third party cannot enforce a contract in their own right, but may enforce it in another capacity, such as personal representative of a contracting party.
facts: A coal merchant transferred his business to his nephew, who promised to pay a weekly sum to the merchant's widow after his death. The nephew paid once and stopped.
held: The widow could not sue in her own right, but as administratrix of her husband's estate she obtained specific performance of the nephew's promise.

name: Derry v Peek
subject: Contracts
principle: A false statement is fraudulent if made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly, careless whether it is true or false.
facts: A company prospectus said it had the right to use steam-powered trams. The directors honestly believed the necessary consent would be given as a formality, but it was refused.
held: The directors were not liable in deceit, because they honestly believed the statement. Lord Herschell's definition of fraud remains the test.

name: Redgrave v Hurd
subject: Contracts
principle: A misrepresentee who relied on the statement may rescind even though they could have discovered the truth with reasonable care.
facts: A solicitor selling his practice misstated its income. The buyer was offered papers that would have shown the truth but did not examine them closely.
held: The buyer could rescind. That he could have found out the truth was no defence.

name: Bisset v Wilkinson
subject: Contracts
principle: An honestly held statement of opinion is not a misrepresentation of fact.
facts: A seller of land that had never been used as a sheep farm said he believed it could carry 2,000 sheep. It could not.
held: No misrepresentation. Both parties knew the land had not been farmed for sheep, so the statement was an honest opinion, not a statement of fact.

name: Edgington v Fitzmaurice
subject: Contracts
principle: A misstatement of present intention is a misstatement of fact; and the misrepresentation need only be one of the inducing causes.
facts: Directors invited loans by saying the money would be used to improve the company's buildings, when they really meant to pay off pressing debts.
held: This was a misrepresentation of fact. Bowen LJ said that the state of a man's mind is as much a fact as the state of his digestion.

name: With v O'Flanagan
subject: Contracts
principle: A statement that was true when made but becomes false before the contract is concluded must be corrected; failing to do so is a misrepresentation.
facts: A doctor selling his medical practice correctly stated its income. By the time of the sale, months later, the practice had largely disappeared because of his illness.
held: The buyer could rescind. The representation was treated as continuing until the contract, and it had become false.

name: Bell v Lever Brothers Ltd
subject: Contracts
principle: A common mistake as to quality makes a contract void only if it makes the subject matter essentially different from what it was believed to be.
facts: Lever Brothers paid two executives large sums to end their service contracts early, then discovered breaches of duty that would have allowed it to dismiss them without paying anything.
held: The agreements were not void. The mistake about their quality was not fundamental enough.

name: Cundy v Lindsay
subject: Contracts
principle: Where parties deal at a distance and the identity of the other party is crucial, a mistake as to identity can make the contract void.
facts: A rogue named Blenkarn ordered goods by letter from a similar address, signing so that his name looked like Blenkiron & Co, a firm the sellers knew. He resold the goods to Cundy.
held: The contract was void, because the sellers intended to deal only with Blenkiron & Co. No title passed to the rogue, and so none passed to Cundy.

name: Phillips v Brooks Ltd
subject: Contracts
principle: In face-to-face dealings there is a presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person physically present, so the contract is voidable, not void.
facts: A rogue in a jeweller's shop claimed to be Sir George Bullough and was allowed to take a ring on credit. He pledged it with a pawnbroker.
held: The contract was only voidable for fraud. The pawnbroker obtained good title before it was avoided.

name: Smith v Hughes
subject: Contracts
principle: Agreement is judged objectively; a party's mistake about quality does not avoid the contract unless the mistake is about the terms and is known to the other party.
facts: A buyer bought oats after seeing a sample, believing they were old oats. They were new oats, which were unsuitable for his horses.
held: A new trial was ordered. If the buyer was merely mistaken about the quality, the contract stood. Only if the seller knew the buyer thought old oats were promised could the buyer escape.

name: Raffles v Wichelhaus
subject: Contracts
principle: Where the terms are latently ambiguous and each party reasonably means something different, there may be no agreement at all.
facts: Cotton was to arrive on a ship called the Peerless sailing from Bombay. There were two ships of that name, sailing in October and December, and each party had a different one in mind.
held: The buyer was allowed to rely on the ambiguity. There was no consensus, so no binding contract.

name: Barton v Armstrong
subject: Contracts
principle: A contract made under threats to the person is voidable if the threats were a reason for entering it, even if not the only reason.
facts: Armstrong threatened to have Barton killed unless Barton's company agreed to buy out Armstrong's interest on generous terms. Barton signed, partly for commercial reasons.
held: Barton could avoid the deed. It was enough that the threats contributed to his decision to sign.

name: Pao On v Lau Yiu Long
subject: Contracts
principle: Economic duress requires coercion of the will that vitiates consent; ordinary commercial pressure is not enough.
facts: The Pao On parties refused to complete a share deal unless the Lau parties gave a guarantee against a fall in the share price. The Laus agreed, to avoid delay and loss of public confidence.
held: The guarantee was enforceable. The pressure was commercial, not duress. The case also restates when an act done before a promise can count as consideration.

name: Allcard v Skinner
subject: Contracts
principle: Gifts made under the influence of a relationship of trust and confidence can be set aside, but the right may be lost by delay (laches).
facts: Miss Allcard joined a religious sisterhood bound by vows of poverty and obedience, and gave it most of her property without independent advice. She left, and six years later sought to recover the gifts.
held: The gifts were made under undue influence, but she had waited too long after leaving the order, so she could not recover them.

name: Lloyds Bank Ltd v Bundy
subject: Contracts
principle: Where a relationship of trust and confidence exists and the bank gains an advantage without the customer having independent advice, the transaction may be set aside for undue influence.
facts: An elderly farmer charged his house, his only asset, to the bank to secure his son's failing business debts, relying on the bank manager's advice.
held: The charge was set aside for undue influence. Lord Denning's wider theory of 'inequality of bargaining power' was later rejected by the House of Lords in National Westminster Bank v Morgan.

name: Royal Bank of Scotland plc v Etridge (No 2)
subject: Contracts
principle: A lender is put on inquiry whenever a wife stands surety for her husband's debts, and must take reasonable steps, usually independent legal advice, to ensure she understands the transaction.
facts: Eight conjoined appeals in which wives had charged the family home to secure their husbands' business debts and later claimed undue influence.
held: The House of Lords restated the law of undue influence and set out the steps banks and solicitors must take, such as a face-to-face meeting with the wife without the husband present.

name: Taylor v Caldwell
subject: Contracts
principle: A contract is discharged where performance becomes impossible because the subject matter is destroyed without the fault of either party.
facts: A music hall was hired for a series of concerts. Before the first concert it was destroyed by fire.
held: Both parties were excused. The contract was subject to an implied condition that the hall would continue to exist.

name: Krell v Henry
subject: Contracts
principle: A contract may be frustrated where an event destroys its common foundation or purpose, even though performance is still physically possible.
facts: A flat was hired for two days to watch the coronation procession of Edward VII. The procession was cancelled because the King was ill.
held: The contract was frustrated. Viewing the procession was the foundation of the contract for both parties.

name: Davis Contractors Ltd v Fareham Urban District Council
subject: Contracts
principle: Frustration requires performance to become radically different from what was undertaken; mere hardship, delay or extra cost is not enough.
facts: Builders agreed to build 78 houses in eight months for a fixed price. Labour shortages meant the work took 22 months and cost much more.
held: The contract was not frustrated. The work was the same, only more onerous, so the builders were held to the agreed price.

name: Cutter v Powell
subject: Contracts
principle: Under an entire contract, payment is due only on complete performance; partial performance earns nothing.
facts: A sailor was to be paid a lump sum provided he served as second mate for the whole voyage from Jamaica to Liverpool. He died about seven weeks before the ship arrived.
held: His widow could recover nothing. Completing the voyage was a condition of payment.

name: Hochster v De la Tour
subject: Contracts
principle: Where one party repudiates before performance is due, the other may sue at once for anticipatory breach.
facts: A courier was engaged to accompany the defendant on a European tour starting on 1 June. In May the defendant said he no longer needed him, and the courier sued before 1 June.
held: The courier could sue immediately. He did not have to wait until the date of performance.

name: Hadley v Baxendale
subject: Contracts
principle: Damages for breach of contract are recoverable for losses arising naturally from the breach, or within the parties' reasonable contemplation when they contracted.
facts: A mill's crankshaft broke and was sent to engineers by carrier to be copied. The carrier delayed delivery, and the mill stood idle for longer.
held: The mill owners could not recover lost profits. The carrier did not know the mill would be idle without the shaft, so the loss was too remote.

name: R v Woollin
subject: Criminal Law
principle: A jury may find intention where death or serious harm was a virtual certainty from the defendant's act and the defendant appreciated that.
facts: The defendant lost his temper and threw his three-month-old son towards a pram. The child hit a hard surface and died.
held: His murder conviction was quashed and replaced with manslaughter, because the jury had been directed on 'substantial risk' rather than virtual certainty.

name: R v Cunningham
subject: Criminal Law
principle: 'Maliciously' in a statute requires intention or subjective recklessness: the defendant must have foreseen the risk of the harm and gone on to take it.
facts: The defendant tore a gas meter from the wall of an empty house to steal the money in it. Gas escaped into the house next door and partly asphyxiated a woman.
held: His conviction was quashed, because the jury was not asked whether he had foreseen that someone might be harmed by escaping gas.

name: R v Miller
subject: Criminal Law
principle: A person who unwittingly creates a dangerous situation, and becomes aware of it, comes under a duty to take reasonable steps to counteract it.
facts: A squatter fell asleep holding a lit cigarette. He woke to find the mattress on fire, moved to another room and went back to sleep. The house was damaged.
held: His conviction for arson was upheld, because he failed to act once he became aware of the danger he had created.

name: R v Pittwood
subject: Criminal Law
principle: A contractual duty can create a duty to act that is owed to the public, and failing to perform it can found criminal liability.
facts: A railway gatekeeper went to lunch leaving a level-crossing gate open. A cart crossing the line was hit by a train and a man was killed.
held: He was guilty of manslaughter. His contract of employment imposed a duty for the protection of the public who used the crossing.

name: R v Dudley and Stephens
subject: Criminal Law
principle: Necessity is not a defence to murder.
facts: After a shipwreck, three men and a cabin boy were adrift without food. After many days two of the men killed the weakened boy and ate him to survive.
held: They were guilty of murder. The death sentence was later commuted to six months' imprisonment.

name: R v Brown
subject: Criminal Law
principle: Consent is not a defence to actual bodily harm or wounding unless the activity falls within a recognised public-interest exception.
facts: A group of men took part, in private and with consent, in sado-masochistic activities that caused injuries.
held: Their convictions were upheld. Consent was no defence on public-policy grounds.

name: R v Olugboja
subject: Criminal Law
principle: There is a difference between real consent and mere submission; whether there was consent is for the jury, applying the ordinary meaning of the word.
facts: A young woman, who had already been raped by the defendant's companion, did not resist when the defendant had intercourse with her, out of fear.
held: The conviction was upheld. Consent is not limited to cases of force or fear of force, and submission is not necessarily consent.

name: R v R
subject: Criminal Law
principle: A husband can be guilty of raping his wife; the common law marital exemption no longer represents the law.
facts: A husband forced his estranged wife to have intercourse after she had left the matrimonial home.
held: His conviction was upheld. Marriage does not imply irrevocable consent to intercourse.

name: R v Clarence
subject: Criminal Law
principle: (Historical) Consent to intercourse was not vitiated by non-disclosure of a sexually transmitted disease. The case has since been overruled on this point.
facts: A husband who knew he had gonorrhoea had intercourse with his wife without telling her, and infected her.
held: His convictions for inflicting grievous bodily harm and assault were quashed. The Court of Appeal later departed from Clarence in R v Dica (2004), holding that reckless transmission can be an offence.

name: Re Akoto
subject: Constitutional Law
principle: Under the 1960 Constitution, the President's declaration of fundamental principles on assuming office did not create a bill of rights enforceable by the courts.
facts: Baffuor Osei Akoto and others were detained under the Preventive Detention Act 1958 and applied for habeas corpus, arguing that the Act and their detention were unconstitutional.
held: The Supreme Court upheld the detention and the Act. The declaration in article 13 imposed a moral obligation on the President, not a legal one. The decision is widely criticised and contrasted with the justiciable rights in the 1992 Constitution.

name: Tuffuor v Attorney-General
court: Court of Appeal (sitting as Supreme Court)
subject: Constitutional Law
principle: The Constitution is the supreme law and must be interpreted as a living document, according to its spirit as well as its letter.
facts: After the 1979 Constitution came into force, Parliament refused to approve the nomination of the serving Chief Justice, Apaloo, as Chief Justice. The plaintiff challenged the position.
held: Under the transitional provisions, the serving Chief Justice continued in office without fresh approval by Parliament. Sowah JA's description of the Constitution as a living organism is often quoted.

name: New Patriotic Party v Attorney-General (31st December case)
subject: Constitutional Law
principle: Celebrating with public funds the overthrow of a constitutionally elected government is inconsistent with the 1992 Constitution.
facts: The government declared 31 December, the anniversary of the 1981 coup, a public holiday and planned to celebrate it with public funds. The NPP challenged this in the Supreme Court.
held: The Supreme Court held the celebration with public funds was inconsistent with the spirit and letter of the Constitution, which forbids the overthrow of constitutional government.

name: New Patriotic Party v Inspector-General of Police
subject: Constitutional Law
principle: A legal requirement to obtain a police permit before holding a public meeting or procession unconstitutionally restricts freedom of assembly.
facts: The NPP challenged provisions of the Public Order Decree 1972 (NRCD 68) that required a police permit for processions and public meetings.
held: The provisions were inconsistent with the freedom of assembly guaranteed by article 21 of the 1992 Constitution and were struck down.

name: J. H. Mensah v Attorney-General
subject: Constitutional Law
principle: Ministers of State need the prior approval of Parliament each time a President begins a new term, including ministers carried over from a previous term.
facts: After the 1996 elections, President Rawlings retained ministers from his first term without submitting them to the new Parliament for approval. The Minority Leader challenged this.
held: The Supreme Court held that fresh parliamentary approval was required under article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution.

name: Ahumah-Ocansey v Electoral Commission; Centre for Human Rights & Civil Liberties v Attorney-General
subject: Constitutional Law
principle: Prisoners who are citizens of voting age and of sound mind have a constitutional right to vote, which the Electoral Commission must make arrangements to secure.
facts: The plaintiffs challenged the Electoral Commission's failure to register prisoners to vote.
held: The Supreme Court held that article 42 of the 1992 Constitution gives the right to vote to every citizen of eighteen years and above of sound mind, prisoners included, and directed the Commission to take steps to register them.

name: Dadzie v Kokofu
subject: Land Law
principle: A document executed by an illiterate cannot support a claim unless it is shown to have been interpreted to him, and a customary pledgee of a farm must keep it in good condition.
facts: The plaintiffs, as successors to Kwame Adufo, said he had pledged his cocoa farm to the defendant about sixteen years earlier as security for a loan of £G7 shortly before his death. The defendant claimed it was an outright sale and relied on a written document signed by illiterates, which he made no effort to prove. The native court found a pledge, but the Land Court reversed it.
held: The Supreme Court restored the finding of a pledge. A claim founded on a document executed by an illiterate could not stand without evidence that it had been interpreted to him. The niece who witnessed the transaction could give evidence of it, and being the only witness did not weaken her well-supported testimony. Sixteen years was not too long for a customary pledge, and keeping the farm in good order, or even improving it, is of the essence of a farm pledge.

name: Akwei v Awuletey
subject: Land Law
principle: The Osu Mantse is the proper authority to grant Osu stool lands, but he cannot validly grant quarter or outskirt lands attached to a quarter without first consulting that quarter's head and elders.
facts: An Osu subject sued for title to part of the Maamobi-Kotobabi-Dzorwulu lands under a deed of gift from the acting Osu Mantse. The defendant relied on a later customary grant from the Osu Mankralo, who claimed the land for his Ashanti Blohum quarter. The plaintiff withdrew, but the Osu Mantse continued as co-plaintiff, and the Land Court found for the defendants.
held: The Osu Mantse could carry on the action after the plaintiff withdrew; standing by would have estopped the stool from reopening the title question. He is the proper party to sue and be sued over land vested in the Osu stool, and the proper grantor of it, subject to prior consultation with a quarter's head and elders for quarter and outskirt lands. The disputed land was neither quarter nor outskirt land but Osu stool rural land, which the Mantse and his elders could grant.

name: Kotey v Asare
subject: Land Law
principle: James Town stool land occupied exclusively or predominantly by subjects or grantees of one sub-stool belongs to that sub-stool, and a sale of family land without the principal members' consent is void.
facts: The plaintiff bought land at Lartebiokorshie from Charles Danso, who held it under a 1956 grant from the Alata stool made to him for himself and his family; he sold without his family's knowledge or consent. The defendant was in possession under a purchase from Madam Adorkor, who had a 1952 conveyance from the Sempe stool registered in 1958. Both stools are sub-stools of James Town.
held: Land of the James Town stool belongs to whichever of its three sub-stools (Alata, Sempe, Akumadjey) has its subjects or grantees exclusively or predominantly in occupation. On the evidence, including accomplished facts on neighbouring land, the disputed land was Sempe land, so the defendant's root of title was better. The Sempe conveyance was also earlier in time and earlier registered, so it had priority. Danso's transfer of family land without the principal members' consent was void from the start.

name: James Town (Alata) Stool v Sempe Stool
subject: Land Law
principle: Where no stool can prove original acquisition, each quarter of James Town owns only the land in the exclusive possession of its people; no single quarter holds allodial title to all James Town stool lands.
facts: Alata and Sempe, two quarters of the James Town stool, contested ownership of the lands west of the Korle Lagoon known as Lartebiokorshie. Neither proved original acquisition, so the trial judge gave each stool the parts its subjects occupied, applying the Akue v Ababio IV test. The Court of Appeal held that test inapplicable and varied the judgment wholly in Sempe's favour.
held: The Supreme Court allowed Alata's appeal and restored the trial judgment. James Town's history showed it was made up of three quarters whose property was vested in the James Town Mantse. Each quarter could claim only the land in its exclusive possession, so it was wrong for any one stool to claim allodial title to all James Town lands. The trial judge had applied the correct test, and there was no need to find that one stool owned the whole area.

name: Saaka v Dahali
subject: Land Law
principle: Long possession by a customary licensee does not by itself defeat the true owner's title, and a subject's usufruct in built-on skin land is not extinguished by a later vesting instrument that is not retrospective.
facts: S, a Dagomba, built a house on a Tamale plot granted by the chief in 1920 and later left it in the care of others, including Y and her daughter D. After S died in 1948, Y's family stayed on, D obtained a government tenancy by falsely claiming to be S's next of kin, and a 1963 instrument vested Tamale skin lands in the President. The High Court dismissed the claim of S's daughter.
held: The appeal was allowed. Y and D were licensees, and long undisturbed occupation alone (subject to the Limitation Decree) gave them no title against S or his successor. Having built on skin land, S held a usufruct the skin could not take away without just cause; EI 109 of 1963 did not cover that interest and, being prospective, could not extinguish rights acquired 43 years earlier. D, a caretaker and agent for S, became a trustee of the house for his heir by staying on after his death.

name: Ameoda v Pordier
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool's jurisdiction over land does not necessarily give it a proprietary interest; Ningo lands are owned by families or quarters, not the stool.
facts: The plaintiff's family sued to recover Ningo land from defendants it said were licensees permitted to stay only while they acknowledged the family's title. The defendants claimed the land was Ningo stool land, and the paramount chief was joined but led no evidence. Ollennu J held all Ningo lands were stool lands, rejecting land tenure studies and a 1917 letter by the Ningo mantse tendered by the plaintiff.
held: The appeal was allowed. The trial judge's definition of stool land, any land whose external affairs a stool conducts, was too wide: a jurisdictional interest does not invariably carry ownership. The plaintiff's evidence of original settlement and seven generations of possession was strong, the objective tenure report should not have been rejected without valid reason, and the 1917 letter was an admission against interest. The land belonged to the plaintiff's family, and because the licensees denied its title the family was entitled to possession, an injunction and damages for trespass.

name: Nyaasemhwe v Afibiyesan
subject: Land Law
principle: An allodial owner who lets another farm his land cannot sue the farmer's successors in trespass, and a customary arbitration binds only if the parties voluntarily submitted and agreed beforehand to be bound.
facts: The plaintiff inherited land and allowed Busumprah to farm it; on Busumprah's death the defendants, his successors, carried on farming. The plaintiff complained to the local chief, who summoned the defendants and decided for the plaintiff. When they ignored the decision, the plaintiff sued for title and trespass damages; the lower courts found for him and treated the arbitration as binding.
held: The appeal was allowed. Without a counterclaim by the defendants, the plaintiff could have a declaration of his allodial title and reversionary rights. But he was not in exclusive possession, and absent proof of a mere sowing tenancy, Busumprah's usufruct had passed to the defendants, so the trespass claim failed. Merely attending a chief's meeting, perhaps out of respect, does not prove submission to arbitration. Whether the parties agreed beforehand to be bound is a question of fact, and no such evidence was led, so there was no estoppel.

name: Golightly v Ashrifi
court: Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool "caretaker" holds an interest in the land, not mere custody; outright alienation of stool land needs the prior consent of the stools concerned, publicity, and the consent of those lawfully in occupation.
facts: The Okaikor Churu family had farmed Kokomlemle land near Accra since 1875 with the Gbese stool's permission. In 1942 the Atukpai family, claiming ownership, sold it to purchasers who built on it. The trial judge declared the occupiers possessory owners subject to the Ga, Gbese and Korle stools as allodial owners, and the Atukpai family appealed against recognition of any interest in the Korle priest beyond caretaker.
held: The Privy Council dismissed the appeal. "Caretaker" denotes a person with an interest in the land, not someone looking after it for another. The Korle priest may grant unappropriated land to stool members to farm or build on, but an outright sale needs the prior consent of the Ga, Gbese and Korle stools and publicity to guard against secret disposals. Even the three stools cannot alienate land without the consent of families or strangers lawfully in occupation. A new point is rarely allowed for the first time before the Board.

name: Sasraku v David
subject: Land Law
principle: Customary law can evolve, stool land in Ashanti can be sold, and a customary sale of stool land between natives passes a possessory, usufructuary right rather than unqualified ownership.
facts: A syndicate of Teshie farmers claimed land it said it had bought outright by customary sale from the Chempaw stool with the knowledge of its paramount, the Kokofu stool. A sawmill felling timber under a Kokofu agreement, with Kokofu joined, argued Ashanti land could not be sold and any sale lacked Kokofu's consent. The trial judge declared title for the plaintiff.
held: The appeal was dismissed, but costs were varied. Courts are not limited to customary law as it stood in 1874. Land is saleable in Ashanti, and Kokofu's knowledge and consent were proved. Conveyances void under the Concessions Ordinance still evidenced a customary sale. Such a sale passes a possessory right to enjoy the land and its usufruct, protected as ownership while the family survives and does not abandon the land. Each party should bear its own costs of an abortive earlier hearing, and the counsel fee awarded was excessive.

name: Kwami v Quaynor
subject: Land Law
principle: Quarter land in Osu is granted by the quarter's head and elders, while Osu stool land is granted by the Osu Mantse, who must consult the quarter before granting unalienated outskirt land in its charge.
facts: In 1897 the elders of Osu Alata Quarter granted land to William Addo Quaynor, who held it undisturbed until he died in 1933. That year the Osu Mantse orally granted part of it to Kwami, confirming the grant by deed in 1957. When Quaynor's son stopped Kwami's workers, Kwami sued and lost before Ollennu J, then appealed alleging bias because the judge had acted as counsel in earlier Alata land cases.
held: The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment for Quaynor. The Mantse grants Osu stool land; a quarter's head and elders grant quarter land; for unalienated outskirt land in a quarter's charge the Mantse decides but must first consult the quarter. As the land was a developed area contiguous to and part of Alata Quarter, the 1897 grant was good and the 1933 grant bad. Bias needs substantial grounds, not mere suspicion; the judge's earlier cases involved different parties and land.

name: Ohimen v Adjei
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool holds vacant stool land absolutely as trustee for its subjects, and cannot alienate land occupied by a subject without that subject's prior consent.
facts: A family sued the stool to which it belonged to stop it alienating stool land in the family's possession without the family's agreement. The stool argued that the family was not in possession, or had long abandoned the land, and had acquiesced in the stool's dealings with it so as to be barred from asserting its rights.
held: Ollennu J held that a stool's interest in vacant land is an absolute estate held in trust for its subjects, who may as of right obtain grants of as much as they need or can work. A subject-grantee's interest is a determinable estate he can defend against anyone, including the stool; it passes on death and may be transferred to another subject, but is forfeited by an act denying the stool's title. The stool may avoid such acts and takes abandoned land, but cannot alienate occupied land without the occupier's prior consent.

name: Ngmati v Adetsia
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool acquires title to land only through its subjects' occupation, so it cannot defeat a family whose ancestors first cultivated the land.
facts: The head of a Yilo Krobo family claimed land at Okwenya that his ancestors had first farmed about 200 years earlier, and sued Ningo settlers who had cultivated it without his permission. The settlers said they farmed with the leave of, and paid tolls to, the Manya Krobo stool, whose local caretaker was joined and claimed the land for that stool. No plan of the land was tendered.
held: A plan is very desirable in a trespass claim but not essential if the oral evidence clearly identifies the land. The plaintiff was not estopped, as he had not acquiesced in the defendants acting adversely to his title. Since a stool gets title only through its subjects, and no Manya Krobo subject claimed the land as ancestral property, that stool could not defeat the Yilo Krobo family's proven original cultivation.

name: Nana Hyeaman II v Osei
subject: Land Law
principle: Vesting stool lands in the President in trust for the stools does not strip stools of their inherent ownership rights, so a chief may still sue to challenge a concession over his stool land.
facts: A divisional chief sued to cancel a timber lease over land attached to his stool. The defendants objected that, because the Concessions Act, 1962 (Act 124), s 16 vests such lands in the President in trust for the stools concerned, only the President could bring the action.
held: The objection was dismissed. Act 124 and the Administration of Lands Act, 1962 (Act 123) deal with the same subject and their identical vesting words must be read the same way. Nothing in either Act shows an intention to deprive stools of their inherent ownership; the President's statutory powers run alongside the stools' rights as allodial owners. Until land is lawfully passed to a concessionaire the stool may still deal with it consistently with Act 123, so the occupant could challenge the purported concession.

name: Awuah v Adututu
subject: Land Law
principle: A receipt acknowledging payment for a customary grant is not a registrable instrument, and documents evidencing a customary grant do not change its customary character.
facts: In 1962 the plaintiff paid £110 for forest land granted by the Akwaboa stool, which its emissaries demarcated; he received a stamped receipt stating the size. The stool later took part of the land and gave it to a second defendant. A survey with the same emissaries supported the plaintiff, but the stool rejected it over the rope used. The trial court found for the plaintiff; the High Court reversed, partly because the receipt was unregistered.
held: The appeal was allowed. The stool's rope was not shown to be the one used years before, and the plaintiff's plan followed boundaries pointed out by the stool's own emissaries and matched his boundary owners, so trespass was proved. The receipt, which merely acknowledged payment and gave a size without identifying particulars, was a duly stamped receipt, not a conveyance needing registration under Act 122. Documents made after a customary grant are only evidence of it and do not alter its nature.

name: Yiboe v Duedu
subject: Land Law
principle: A judgment on the extent of a family's usufructuary interest does not make the stool's absolute title res judicata where that title was not in issue in the earlier case.
facts: An Akloba stool had earlier sued a family for trespass and lost, but on appeal the declaration of the family's ownership was deleted because the family had not counterclaimed. The family then sued for title, relying only on the earlier proceedings, and the stool counterclaimed that the land was communal land under its control. The native courts found for the stool.
held: Ollennu J held that the issue was not res judicata. In the first action the stool did not deny the family's usufructuary interest, only that it was exclusive, so the issue then was the nature and limits of that interest. The present dispute concerned absolute title, which was a different issue. The court suggested that had the counterclaim's issue been decided, or relied on by the stool, in the earlier case, the stool would have been estopped from raising it.

name: Bruce v Quarnor
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool cannot grant land already occupied by a subject or grantee without the occupier's consent, and a customary grant takes effect at once and cannot be cut down by a later deed.
facts: The plaintiff had farmed James Town stool land at West Korle Gonno under a customary grant made over 30 years earlier, and later received a deed in 1956. The defendants entered parts of the land claiming later grants or a deed of gift from the stool or its occupant. They argued the plaintiff lacked standing because he had given portions of the land to his children.
held: Under custom a grantor undertakes to secure the grantee's title and must defend it when it is challenged, so the plaintiff was properly before the court even after gifting parts to his children. A customary grant is effective immediately; a later deed may add to it but cannot reduce it. A subject may occupy vacant stool land on an actual or implied grant, and the stool cannot regrant occupied land without the occupier's consent, nor take it back by giving other land instead.

name: Oblee v Armah
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool subject may generally occupy vacant stool land without express permission, is not confined to the purpose for which he took it; a stool grant of land possessed by a subject without his consent is a nullity.
facts: All parties were subjects of the James Town Stool, Accra. The plaintiff relied on a stool grant made about forty years earlier and long possession by farming and building; the defendants relied on later stool grants and argued that land given for farming was forfeited when the plaintiff built on it. The land had been compulsorily acquired under the Accra Town (Lands) Ordinance and later released.
held: Hearsay from the plaintiff's son was not admissible as traditional evidence where direct evidence was available. A subject's use of stool land is not limited to the purpose for which it was taken, so building on farm land caused no forfeiture. On urban outskirt land ripe for development an express stool grant is needed, but the incidents are the same. The later grants to the defendants, made without the plaintiff's consent, were void, and the plaintiff, being in possession, could sue everyone except the government.

name: Budu II v Caesar
subject: Land Law
principle: A customary arbitration requires voluntary submission, prior agreement to accept the award, a judicial hearing of both sides, procedure akin to the Native Court, and publication of the award; mere settlement talks are not arbitration.
facts: Nana Budu claimed a two-square-mile area as stool land against the Caesar family and others. He argued that an earlier dispute had been settled by arbitration under the Omanhene of Akwamu, and that the defendants were estopped because they had let him declare the land as stool land and had not declared their interest under a State Council resolution.
held: None of the elements of a customary arbitration was present; the Omanhene had only tried to negotiate a settlement. The defendants were not estopped by standing by while the land was treated as stool property, since the plaintiff was never shown to have been required to declare it, and an owner may ignore a wrongful inclusion of his land. Non-compliance with the State Council resolution created no estoppel because it was not shown to have the force of law. A stool's purchaser may re-sell without the stool's concurrence.

name: Amatei v Hammond
subject: Land Law
principle: A grant of stool land by an acting chief whose appointment is void is itself void, but a good-faith occupier who acknowledged the stool's title may be protected under the Land Development (Protection of Purchasers) Act, 1960.
facts: The Gyasetse declared the Osu Mankralo destooled and an acting mankralo was appointed, who granted the plaintiff a building plot. The defendant claimed the same plot under an earlier grant from the substantive mankralo but did nothing on it. The plaintiff built on the land in good faith.
held: No charges were preferred against the mankralo, so his purported destoolment breached customary law and natural justice and was of no effect; the acting mankralo's appointment and his grant to the plaintiff were therefore void. Neither party had a valid grant, but the plaintiff was in actual occupation against an intruder. Having acted in good faith and acknowledged the stool's title, he was protected under Act 2 and L.I. 118, which cured the grantor's lack of capacity.

name: Frimpong v Poku
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool subject's customary right to cultivate stool land is not an unlimited licence for indiscriminate cultivation; subjects normally obtain the stool's permission and are given demarcated areas.
facts: The defendant, a stranger, was allowed by the Sankori stool to farm a limited area but spread his crops over a wider area. Offered the chance to pay for the extra land, he could not, and the stool sold it to the plaintiff. By then the defendant had become a Sankori subject; the High Court held that, as a subject, he could occupy vacant stool land, so the sale was invalid.
held: The Supreme Court allowed the plaintiff's appeal. The rule that a subject may farm any amount of stool land does not license indiscriminate cultivation, and in modern conditions limited areas are demarcated for subjects to ensure fair distribution. Separately, because the defendant had not lodged a copy of his notice of intention to appeal within the required month, a statutory condition precedent, his appeal was never properly before the High Court.

name: Nsiah v Asare
subject: Land Law
principle: Under the Public Lands Ordinance, only the Commissioner of Lands may refer rival claims for compensation to the court with jurisdiction; claimants cannot sue each other, and Native Courts lack jurisdiction over such claims.
facts: After the government gave notice to acquire land at Dodowa, both Asare and Nsiah claimed compensation from the Commissioner of Lands. Nsiah then sued Asare in the Shai Native Court for interfering with his land and won; Asare appealed to the Land Court.
held: Making a compensation claim, even when another person also claims, is not an actionable wrong, so the writ disclosed no cause of action. Read as a whole, Nsiah's real claim was to be declared the person entitled to compensation. The Ordinance by implication gives jurisdiction over such claims only to the Lands Division of the Supreme Court and gives the Commissioner alone the right to refer rival claims to it. The Native Court therefore had no jurisdiction and the proceedings were ultra vires.

name: Total Oil Products Ltd v Obeng
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool subject may transfer or lease his usufructuary interest without the stool's consent, and a stool cannot alienate land in a subject's possession without the subject's consent.
facts: A Tafo stool subject sold developed farm land to the first defendant, a stranger, by deeds purporting to convey the fee simple. The first defendant leased it to the plaintiff company. The Tafo stool then ejected the company and granted it a new lease, and the company sued to rescind the first lease and recover money paid.
held: There was no contract with the second defendant, so the claim against him was dismissed as frivolous. Section 75 of the Local Government Ordinance applies only to undeveloped land acquired for nominal consideration, so no council concurrence was needed. Although customary law knows no fee simple, the deeds passed the seller's usufructuary title. A subject's lease of his land needs no stool consent, so the first lease was valid; the stool's lease, made without the possessor's consent, was void.

name: Buor v Beede
court: High Court, Eastern Judicial Division, Land Court
subject: Land Law
principle: A sale of a subject's determinable estate in stool land to a stranger without stool consent is voidable at the stool's instance, not void; acquiescence binds the stool only if it knew its rights were infringed.
facts: The plaintiff sued to redeem a cocoa farm on stool land that his predecessor had pledged. The third defendant, who bought from the second defendant, argued the original transaction was an outright sale, relying on a contemporaneous document calling it a sale. The plaintiff argued any sale to a stool stranger was void without stool consent; the defendants replied that the stool was estopped after thirty years.
held: The original transaction was a pledge, since the document was not a conveyance and its description was rebutted by other evidence. A pledge carries possession and is freely assignable, so the purported sale to the third defendant passed only the pledge. Had it been a sale, lack of stool consent would make it voidable, not void, as with family land. No estoppel arose against the stool because it had no reason to know its residual rights were infringed.

name: Baidoo v Osei
court: High Court, Eastern Judicial Division, Land Court
subject: Land Law
principle: A stool subject who first reduces virgin stool land into cultivation acquires a determinable estate the stool cannot alienate without his consent, and he may alienate it without stool consent if the transferee recognises the stool's title.
facts: The plaintiff, a stool subject, claimed land at Koforidua by first clearing it from virgin forest. The first defendant, a stranger, relied on a 1932 sale from the second defendant, another subject claiming first cultivation, and on a confirmatory lease from the New Juaben Stool in 1948. The Native Court found for the plaintiff, and the defendants appealed.
held: First cultivation gives a subject a usufructuary estate by implied grant, which the stool cannot alienate without his consent. The subject may transfer it without stool consent provided the transferee recognises the stool's superior title and performs customary services, though the stool may lose those services by acquiescence. On the evidence the plaintiff came first, so the stool's lease, based on the mistaken view that the second defendant held the estate, had no effect. The defendants' acts were intermittent and not acquiesced in, so no estoppel ran against the plaintiff.

name: Mansu v Abboye
subject: Land Law
principle: A usufructuary interest in stool land is potentially perpetual; apart from statutory acquisition, it ends only by the holder's consent, abandonment, failure of successors, or proven unrectified breach of customary tenure.
facts: The plaintiff claimed family land at Yarbiw that his ancestors had cleared from virgin forest. The Odikro, claiming allodial title, said the land had reverted to him after being released by the State Farms Corporation, and licensed the defendant to exploit palm trees on it. The circuit court held that the land had reverted to the stool.
held: The appeal was allowed. A usufructuary has exclusive possession and cannot be divested at the stool's whim, nor can the stool grant his land to another without his prior consent. None of the recognised ways of ending the interest was present, and the plaintiff's land was never shown to have been compulsorily acquired. There was therefore no basis for holding that it reverted to the stool on release.

name: Gyamfi v Owusu
subject: Land Law
principle: Stool land must be compulsorily acquired under the Administration of Lands Act, 1962 (Act 123), not Act 125; and stool subjects lack standing to sue over stool property, the Kwan v Nyieni exceptions not extending to stool land.
facts: When the government took the Digya-Kogyae lands of the Kumawu stool for a national park, the Omanhene, a sub-chief and others fraudulently claimed and received the compensation for themselves. Kumawu stool subjects sued for its recovery and won in the High Court; the appellants challenged their standing.
held: The appeal was allowed. Because the land was stool land, Act 123 applied; no instrument of acquisition was made and published under section 7, so there was no legal acquisition and the compensation payment was irregular. The subjects had no standing: under customary law only the stool occupant can sue over stool property, and the court would not extend the family-property exceptions in Kwan v Nyieni to stools. Under section 17 of Act 123 the Minister was the proper party to recover the money.

name: Serwah v Kesse
subject: Land Law
principle: In an action for declaration of title the onus is on the plaintiff and never shifts, but the standard is the civil balance of probabilities, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.
facts: A former Queen Mother of New Juaben claimed that 28 farms on which agricultural grants had been paid to her during her reign were her family property. Her successor said they were stool property. Ollennu J found for the plaintiff, and the successor appealed, arguing title had to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, the court lacked jurisdiction, and the farms merged with stool property because they were not declared on enstoolment.
held: Each ground failed. The plaintiff bears the onus in title cases, but a preponderance of probability suffices, and here she had proved her case strongly. A title claim against a stool claiming the land is not a constitutional matter ousting the courts' jurisdiction under the Courts Act, 1960. Because the Queen Mother's stool was recently created and owned no property with which her own could mix, no pre-enstoolment declaration of her private property was needed.

name: Essien v Duncan
subject: Land Law
principle: Land alienated absolutely escheats to the grantor only if it becomes ownerless; a mere right to escheat is not a title able to defeat a person in long possession.
facts: In the 1890s the defendant's family conveyed land absolutely to Russell; it later passed to Renner, who gave part to the plaintiff in 1936 and put him in possession. The conveyance to Renner could not be found. In 1950 the family re-entered, claiming the land had reverted to them, and the Native (Municipal) Court found for them.
held: Absolutely alienated land escheats only on abandonment or the grantee's death without successor, and neither had occurred. Even if title had not properly reached the plaintiff, the family had parted with their title absolutely, and a possible right of escheat is not enough to defeat possession. Even if they had kept some superior title, their laches barred them from succeeding against the plaintiff in possession.

name: Bukuruwa Stool v Kumawu Stool
subject: Land Law
principle: Only the stool occupant, or when the stool is vacant a regent or person appointed by the stool elders, can sue or be sued over stool property; a judgment against an unauthorised representative does not bind the stool.
facts: Bukuruwa stool sued Kumawu stool for title to land in Kwahu. Kumawu pleaded res judicata based on a 1959 judgment it won against the Bukuruwa Queen Mother as representing the stool. The Bukuruwa stool was vacant at the time, the Queen Mother was destooled before the hearing, and that suit went undefended.
held: A plaintiff suing a person as a stool's representative must prove that person is the regent or caretaker, particularly where the representative does not appear or denies capacity. Being a stool elder, or having joined in executing a stool mortgage, is not proof of authority to represent the stool in litigation. With no evidence of express authority, the 1959 judgment did not bind the Bukuruwa stool, and the plea of res judicata failed.

name: Kwan v Nyieni
subject: Land Law
principle: The head of family is normally the proper person to sue for family property, but any member may sue in special circumstances to preserve the property; a disposition without the principal members' knowledge and consent is void.
facts: The family head and one member mortgaged four family cocoa farms to Nyieni without the knowledge of the principal members. Nyieni later sold the farms under the mortgage. Kwan, a member whom the family had irregularly appointed as a new head, sued to set the sale aside, but the trial judge dismissed the action because Kwan was neither head nor authorised.
held: The appeal was allowed. A member may sue where the property is at risk and the head will not act, where family division stops the head acting, or where the head and principal members are disposing of it for their own benefit, if he shows authority or necessity and sues to preserve the family property. A deed by the head and another member, timeously proved to lack the principal members' knowledge and consent, is void, so the mortgage and the sale under it passed no title.

name: Allotey v Abrahams
court: High Court, Eastern Judicial Division, Land Court
subject: Land Law
principle: No valid disposal of stool or family land is possible without the occupant's or head's consent; a conveyance he executes with principal elders, stated to have the required consents, is valid until those challenging it prove otherwise.
facts: The plaintiffs held Sempe Stool land under a 1946 conveyance executed by the Sempe Mantse and some elders, stated to be with the elders' consent. The defendant, claiming to be the Sempe Stool Father, said his consent was essential, that paying stool debts made him owner of stool property, and that an earlier Native Court judgment barred the Mantse from alienating stool land.
held: Paying a stool's debts does not subrogate the payer to stool property. The defendant was not the Stool Father, and even if he held a stool office he had stood aside from stool affairs for years and could not challenge decisions for want of his concurrence. A conveyance not shown to have the occupant's consent is prima facie ineffective, though consent can be proved otherwise. One executed by the occupant with elders and reciting the required consents stands unless the aggrieved persons promptly prove the consents were missing.

name: Amankwanor v Asare
subject: Land Law
principle: There is no presumption that an illiterate understood a document he executed; and a document purporting to convey stool land does not bind the stool unless the elders, or at least the linguist, are parties to it.
facts: The plaintiff sued the defendant for trespass to a cocoa farm at Krodua, which had been divided between the plaintiff's predecessor and the then Odikro. The defendant relied on exhibit A, an English document said to have been given by the illiterate present Odikro, evidencing a sale to the defendant's father. The local court found for the plaintiff, but the High Court reversed.
held: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal. Whoever seeks to bind an illiterate to a document must prove it was properly explained and understood, and the defendant called neither the letter writer nor the witnesses, so he failed to do so. Exhibit A also could not bind the stool, because under customary law a document conveying stool land needs the elders, or at least the linguist, as parties.

name: Nunekpeku v Ametepe
subject: Land Law
principle: A family member occupying vacant family land acquires a limited right individual members cannot defeat; if he alienates part without consent, the family must sue the purchaser or first resolve at a meeting to dispossess him.
facts: The defendant occupied part of Agbeve family land at Bawe and, together with a junior family member, sold a portion to a stranger. The family head and principal members sued to eject him from the land, claiming he was not a family member but a licensee and that his unauthorised dealing forfeited his holding. A local court ordered his ejection and he appealed.
held: The appeal succeeded. The plaintiffs' own admissions showed the defendant belonged to the family through his mother, so he was entitled to occupy vacant family land and could not be ejected at the will of individual members. Where a member alienates family land without reference to the family, its remedy is an action against the purchaser, or a family meeting deciding to take back the member's portion, after which he becomes a trespasser if he refuses to yield. No such meeting had been held, so the action was premature and disclosed no cause of action.

name: Larbi v Cato
subject: Land Law
principle: A house becomes family property through members' contributions only if the contribution is real and the builder accepts it as building for the family; family-funded education does not make a member's later earnings family property.
facts: A man built a house in Accra on self-acquired land, later extended it, gave it to his son by deed of gift and confirmed the gift in his will. After his death his brother, as family head, sued the widow and brother-in-law claiming the house was family property, alleging family members helped finance it and that the deceased was educated with family funds. Ollennu J dismissed the claim and the plaintiff appealed.
held: Customary law imposes no duty on a son educated with family support to repay it, and his earnings do not become family profits. Contributing members share in a building only where the builder, by accepting their help, recognises he is building a family house; a loan or a member's own share of a family fund is different. The presumption of family ownership is rebuttable, and the onus shifts once the person is shown to have dealt with the property as his own or received it by gift or will. A contribution need not be large but must be real.

name: Amissah-Abadoo v Abadoo
subject: Land Law
principle: A member who builds with his own resources on land in the family's effective occupation takes only a life interest in the house, which he cannot devise; minor domestic help by relatives does not make it family property.
facts: A built a house with his own means, and with family consent, on land his father had given by deed to A's mother and her children and their heirs and assigns as family property. His mother supervised the building and his sister cooked for him. A devised the house, and a plot redeemed from his sister, to his widow and children. His brother, as matrilineal family head, sued the widow claiming both as family property.
held: A plaintiff suing in a particular capacity must prove it once challenged; only the sister's children could claim the redeemed plot, so that claim failed for want of capacity. The mother's supervision and the sister's cooking were not substantial enough to give the house a family character. But since the family was in effective occupation of the land, A held only a life interest and could not devise the house. The words heirs and assigns in the deed were words of limitation, making the land the joint property of the donee family.

name: Nkonnua v Anaafi
subject: Land Law
principle: Property a chief develops from family land, or acquires with the help of members of his family, is family property and does not become stool property merely because he was on the stool at the time.
facts: The queen-mother and head of a royal family claimed a cocoa farm that her uncle had developed from a family farmstead while he occupied the Osenase stool. The elders knew he treated the farm as his own; it was never placed under the stool treasury and was left off the inventory of stool property handed over when he abdicated. His son, the current occupant of the stool, claimed it as stool property.
held: The court found for the plaintiff. The land already belonged to the royal family before the chief took it over, so the farm he made on it was family property, all the more so since he only developed an existing family farmstead. Property acquired with the help of a family member becomes family property, so a chief who acquires property with such help holds it as family, not stool, property. The plaintiff had helped him physically and financially to make the farm.

name: Yoguo v Agyekum
subject: Land Law
principle: A valid customary gift of land needs a transfer ceremony, publicity, libation and aseda; property acquired from a common purse of family members becomes family property on their deaths unless partitioned.
facts: Two children of B claimed a house at Yonso, saying their father built it on land acquired from the Yonso stool and gave it to them, with aseda before witnesses. B's family said B and his elder brother A built it together on family land and that no valid gift was made. The trial judge found for the children and the family appealed.
held: By a majority the appeal was allowed. The children had not proved the land came from the stool: what their father told them was hearsay, not tradition, and no stool elder was called. Under custom, property acquired from a common purse kept by A and B was family property and, never having been partitioned, became full family property on their deaths. The children also failed to prove the elements of a customary gift: a transfer ceremony, publication to the living and the dead, libation and aseda. Lassey JSC dissented on the burden of proof.

name: Adjei v Appiagyei
subject: Land Law
principle: A family head's dealing with family property without the family's concurrence is voidable, not void; it is set aside only if the family did not acquiesce, acted promptly and diligently, and the innocent party can be restored.
facts: Family land was mortgaged by the customary successor of a deceased member, with the deed also signed by a man described as family head and two others as members. A family representative sued to cancel the mortgage, alleging fraud and lack of family consent. The present defendant, the original mortgagee's successor, said proper searches were made in good faith, and the Asantehene had consented in writing. The trial court found for the plaintiff.
held: A transaction by a family head affecting family property without the family's assent is voidable at the family's instance. It will be avoided only if the family shows it did not acquiesce, acted timeously and diligently, and the innocent party can be put back in his former position. A ruling that someone is or is not a family member does not bind non-parties. The plaintiff proved none of the required matters and had not pleaded or proved fraud with enough particularity, so there was no case for the defendant to answer.

name: Attah v Aidoo
subject: Land Law
principle: A person impeaching an alienation of family property must prove the principal members did not consent; a pledgor's equity of redemption can be attached and sold in execution.
facts: A customary successor pledged six family farms to raise money for family funeral expenses. On default, a creditor obtained judgment and the farms were seized and sold to the other pledgee, who had held them for about twelve years. The new successor sued for a declaration that the pledge and sale were unlawful and for the sale to be set aside.
held: The action was dismissed. The plaintiff bore the burden of proving that the principal elders had not consented and failed to do so; after about twelve years of possession by the buyer it was too late for the family to complain. The rules of court allowed a judgment debtor's immovable property, including his equity of redemption, to be attached. The pledgee could buy the farms; by acquiring the equity of redemption he stood in the pledgor's shoes, and the pledgor's right to redeem ended, despite the customary maxim once a pledge always a pledge.

name: Akrofi v Otenge
subject: Land Law
