principle: Where a family head claims that property sold in execution against a member was family property, the court must view the claim with great caution and require a high degree of proof on the balance of probabilities.
facts: A family head sued to set aside the auction sale of a farm sold to satisfy a judgment debt against G, a family member, claiming the farm was family property. G had pledged the farm years after supposedly handing it over, the auction was widely advertised without the family acting, and G was not called as a witness. The High Court found for the plaintiff, but the Court of Appeal reversed.
held: The appeal was dismissed. On capacity the plaintiff won: his credible evidence, backed by a family member, was unanswered, and the defendants called no evidence on who the head was. But judgment debtors could too easily shelter behind their families, so a family's claim to property sold in execution must be examined with extreme caution and a high degree of proof required. The plaintiff failed to prove family ownership; the probabilities were that the farm was G's and that the action was brought in collusion with him.

name: Lamptey v Neequaye
subject: Land Law
principle: Eligibility to succeed is not a right to succeed; until a successor is properly chosen at a family meeting, the head of family manages the estate, and members of the same class of successors share it equally.
facts: A's children and uterine grandchildren disputed a Kaneshie house A had rented from the Housing Department. After A's death her eldest daughter L had the tenancy put in her name, took up an option for a rebuilt house and signed the lease. A's son, claiming to be successor, sued his relatives for a declaration that he and his co-plaintiff were exclusively entitled and for their ejectment.
held: The house remained A's self-acquired property: L acted as caretaker of the immediate family, so her improvements were presumed made for the family. The plaintiffs and defendants were in the same class of successors and had equal rights; postponement of enjoyment does not operate within one class. The second plaintiff showed no family meeting had chosen him, and a head of family cannot appoint or confirm a successor alone. The head of the wider family was entitled to manage the estate, so the plaintiffs lacked locus standi.

name: Daatsin v Amissah
subject: Land Law
principle: A family is not liable for the debts of a deceased member, so the family head cannot be sued for them; a head suing in a representative capacity is personally liable for costs.
facts: A member of one branch of a family owed money to a member of another branch. After both died, the head of the creditor's branch sued the head of the debtor's branch for the debt. The local court and the magistrate found for the plaintiff, and the defendant appealed to the High Court.
held: The appeal succeeded. The family of a deceased person is not liable for his debts, so an action for them cannot be brought against the family head. In any case no cause of action was shown, because the creditor's estate passed to his own matrilineal family, whose head alone could sue. A head of family suing in a representative capacity is personally liable for costs awarded against him.

name: Welbeck v M Captan Ltd
subject: Land Law
principle: A family may appoint a new head at any time in due form; absent principal members who were invited cannot invalidate the meeting, and the person attacking a family decision must prove the meeting was unrepresentative.
facts: The plaintiff, appointed caretaker of family property after the former head was relieved of office, sued the lessee of family houses for rent. The former head claimed he had been reappointed head at a later meeting, which some principal members supporting the plaintiff refused to attend. The plaintiff argued the meeting was void because the two branches had not been reconciled and principal members were absent.
held: On the facts both branches were represented at the meeting that appointed the former head, so no prior reconciliation was needed. A family may make a fresh appointment to the headship at any time if done in proper form. The absence of principal members can make a meeting's decisions void, but not where they were invited and chose not to come. A member who challenges a family decision as unrepresentative bears the burden of proving it.

name: Banahene v Adinkra
subject: Land Law
principle: A duly appointed successor may recover ancestral family farms from junior members who hold them only as caretakers; evidence corroborated by an opponent's witness should be preferred unless shown to be incredible.
facts: A, who had inherited three ancestral farms as successor and head of family, died intestate. The plaintiff was elected successor at a family meeting chaired by the local Gyasehene and attended by the principal members. Junior members whom A had made caretakers of the farms disputed his election and refused to hand them over. The district court found for the plaintiff but the High Court reversed.
held: The appeal was allowed. The plaintiff's account of his election was fully corroborated by the defendants' own key witness, so the High Court should not have overturned the magistrate's acceptance of it. A neutral chief or respected person may properly chair a family meeting at the family's request, especially where there is dissension. The plaintiff bore the general burden, but the defendants carried the burden on their plea of ignorance and failed. As they were not shown to enjoy the farms in their own right, they could not resist the successor's right to manage them.

name: Hervie v Tamakloe
subject: Land Law
principle: No one becomes head of family automatically; the elders appoint the most suitable person, expressly or by accepting his acts as head, and may look outside the usual line of descent.
facts: In a patrilineal area, the plaintiff, suing as family head, sought damages for trespass and an injunction against the defendants, who had entered family creeks. The defendants denied he was head or even of the male line and claimed rights as members. His evidence of descent was contradictory and conflicted with his earlier testimony, and he gave no evidence of being appointed head.
held: Headship is neither automatic nor a matter of right; like a successor, the head is chosen by the elders, formally or by their acceptance and support of his acts as head. The elders may go outside the natural line, choosing from the maternal line in a patrilineal area if no suitable male-line candidate exists. The plaintiff was not of the male line, which was not fatal by itself, but having had his headship challenged he failed to prove any appointment, so his claim failed.

name: Quagraine v Edu
subject: Land Law
principle: A customary successor can be removed only at a meeting fully representative of the wider family; the immediate family has beneficial enjoyment of the estate while the wider family's rights are postponed.
facts: Apprey died intestate, survived by his mother and two uterine brothers, one of whom, the plaintiff, was made his successor. The head of the wider family, unhappy with his management, called a meeting to which some branches were not invited, removed him in his absence, and posted notices on seven estate houses telling tenants not to pay him rent. The plaintiff sued for trespass and a perpetual injunction.
held: The removal was invalid because the meeting did not represent the whole wider family. The immediate family, headed by the plaintiff, was entitled to the beneficial enjoyment of the estate; the wider family's rights were postponed until the immediate family died out. But the head of the wider family had a duty to protect family property and acted in good faith in posting the notices, so there was no trespass, and an injunction stopping him from protecting the property would be contrary to custom.

name: Abakah v Ambradu
subject: Land Law
principle: A head of family can be removed only by the principal members after notice of the complaint, at a meeting of which all sectional heads were notified; absence for a customary family funeral is justified.
facts: Elders dissatisfied with the long-serving head's management of family property sent him charges and called him to a meeting. He attended the first meeting but left, saying it was improperly constituted. At a later meeting he was absent attending a family funeral; the charges were found proved, he was removed and replaced. The new head sued for an injunction and the family documents, and the High Court dismissed the claim.
held: The appeal was dismissed. The power to remove a head lies with the principal members, but where not all sectional heads were notified, those present cannot bind the rest unless they acquiesce. A head may sometimes be removed in his absence, but not where he is away because custom required him at a family funeral. He cannot be removed without a complaint and a summons to answer it. The notice need not say the purpose is to depose him, since that depends on the charges being proved.

name: Allotey v Quarcoo
subject: Land Law
principle: Whether a family head should be deposed is for the family; courts interfere only for a substantial denial of justice, and the challenger must plead and prove specific grounds of invalidity.
facts: The respondent, deposed as joint head of family at a family meeting, sued for a declaration that he remained head but pleaded no specific grounds of invalidity. The trial judge confined the trial to whether the meeting ended abruptly, but then raised eight new issues himself, including voting procedure and natural justice, and reinstated the respondent.
held: The appeal was allowed. A court may not build a case of its own or decide issues neither pleaded nor fairly met by the other side. The burden of alleging and proving specific grounds for invalidating a family decision to appoint or remove a head rests on the member who challenges it. The merits of deposing a head at a fully representative, duly notified meeting are for the family; courts have only a limited supervisory role and intervene only on a complete or substantial denial of justice, which must be pleaded with particulars.

name: Hansen v Ankrah
subject: Land Law
principle: A serving head of family cannot be sued in court for an account by family members; he answers for his stewardship to the family at a family meeting, which may remove him.
facts: Two branch heads of a family sued the overall head and another branch head for an account of family money, including compulsory acquisition compensation the overall head had paid into his personal account. The defendants objected that they were not accountable in court. The High Court overruled the objection, but the Court of Appeal held the head was not accountable to the plaintiffs and dismissed the suit.
held: By a majority the appeal was dismissed. The customary rule that a sitting head of family is not accountable in court to a member's writ was held reasonable, since the head must be able to manage family affairs. He is accountable to the family: an aggrieved member should raise the complaint with the principal members, who may call a meeting, hear the charges and remove him if serious misconduct such as misappropriation is proved. Removal was a more effective remedy than a lengthy lawsuit, so the action was incompetent. Apaloo CJ and Taylor JSC dissented.

name: Quartey v Martey
subject: Land Law
principle: At customary law, property a man acquires with his wife's and children's assistance is his individual property; on his intestacy it becomes family property, and a widow has a right only to maintenance, not a share.
facts: A widow married under customary law sued her late husband's relatives for the balance of his funeral expenses she had paid and for a one-third share of his cattle, house and bank money. She said a customary widow takes one-third of an intestate's estate, and that she had helped him acquire the property. The defendants disputed the marriage and her authority to incur the funeral costs.
held: Ollennu J found that she was a lawful customary wife but rejected her claim to a one-third share. Help from a wife and children in a man's work is part of their customary duty, so what he acquires with it remains his own. Property bought with proceeds of family property is itself family property. On intestacy self-acquired property passes to the family, no member takes a fixed share, and the widow is entitled only to maintenance. Funeral expenses are the family's responsibility and are claimed from the head of family or the successor.

name: Clerk v Clerk
subject: Land Law
principle: A wife's uncertain contribution to a house does not give her an equitable interest, but a husband cannot eject his wife from the matrimonial home while the marriage subsists, especially when he is in desertion.
facts: The parties married under the Marriage Ordinance and the marriage still subsisted, but they lived apart. The husband, who had bought the land with his own money and in his own name, asked the wife to leave the house so he could extend and let it. She sought an injunction, claiming a beneficial interest from her money and labour and a right to stay in the matrimonial home. He counterclaimed for title and possession.
held: Campbell J held that the wife's contribution was too uncertain to found an equitable interest without speculation. Since Ghanaian legislation had no equivalent of section 17 of the English 1882 Act, spouses' property rights during their lives were governed by customary law, under which a husband's property built with his wife's help stays his. However, at common law, and similarly at customary law, a husband cannot eject his wife from the matrimonial home while the marriage lasts, and this applies with greater force where he is in desertion.

name: Abebreseh v Kaah
subject: Land Law
principle: Where a customary wife's contribution to the matrimonial home goes well beyond the ordinary help custom expects, she may be declared joint owner, even though she cannot put a figure on it.
facts: A wealthy trader wife paid half the price of the plot, bought timber and other materials, supervised the work and maintained the family while her husband built their house. After he died intestate, his customary successor took out letters of administration alone and, without telling the family, sold the house. The buyer's nominee gave the widow notice to quit, and she sued to have the sale declared void.
held: Sarkodee J granted the declaration and held the sale void. Although she could not quantify her contribution, it was clearly substantial, and commercial standards of proof do not apply between spouses. The customary rule that a husband owns property acquired with his wife's help rests on the wife depending on him, which was not the case here, and her contribution far exceeded customary assistance. Customary law does not prohibit joint ownership between spouses, so she was a joint owner. Quartey v Martey was distinguished.

name: Anang v Tagoe
subject: Land Law
principle: Where a wife contributes to building a matrimonial home believing it to be joint property, equity will make that belief good, even if the exact amount of her contribution is not proved.
facts: A wife sued for a declaration that she jointly owned a house built on land bought in her husband's name. She had given money for materials, fed the workers, organised block making and supervised building while he, a police officer, was posted outside Accra. He denied any help, relied on the indenture and receipts in his name, and counterclaimed for sole ownership. His brother was substituted when he died.
held: Brobbey J declared the wife a joint owner. The husband had led her to believe, as a letter confirmed, that the house was for them both and their children, and she spent her own money and effort on that basis. The receipts showed only his share of what was a joint effort. Equity would not let him keep the benefit of her contributions and enrich himself unjustly. Failure to prove the precise extent of her contribution was no bar, since dealings between spouses are not documented like commercial ones. Achiampong v Achiampong applied.

name: In re Antubam; Quaico v Fosu
subject: Land Law
principle: Under Akan custom the widows and children of an intestate hold an interest in his self-acquired immovable property equivalent to a determinable life tenancy, subject to which the maternal family succeeds.
facts: An Akan man died intestate, leaving two widows and nine children. The head of his family took out an originating summons to determine whether the widows and children, and the family, had any interest in his self-acquired property. The family argued the estate belonged wholly to the family, with the widows and children entitled only to maintenance and residence at the successor's discretion.
held: Archer J held that the widows and children had an interest akin to a determinable life tenancy. Widows may live in the deceased's houses during widowhood, children for life subject to good behaviour, and both may share in income from the property. The head of family or successor must maintain them by adequate allowances. The property becomes family property, with the maternal family succeeding subject to these interests. In obiter remarks he said customary law must develop and children cannot be shut out of their father's property.

name: Hayford v Moses
subject: Land Law
principle: A customary widow and her children have a possessory life interest in the deceased's self-acquired home that ranks ahead of the successor, and the successor must maintain them.
facts: After a man died intestate owning a block of six flats, his widow stayed in the family flat and collected rent from two others to keep herself and their children. The customary successor, who held letters of administration alone, sued for the keys and an account of the rents. While the case was pending, the widow was made a joint administrator under section 77 of the Administration of Estates Act, 1961.
held: Sarkodee J dismissed the action. Her later grant of letters related back to the death because she had acted for the benefit of the estate, so she did not have to account. The possessory life interest of the widow and children ranks ahead of the successor's and the family's rights, so they could keep the whole flat. The successor inherits the husband's duty to house and maintain them. Having failed to do so, he had made the widow an agent of necessity, entitled to be repaid from the estate.

name: Yeboah v Kwakye
subject: Land Law
principle: A family member who farms vacant family land, even with his own resources, gets only a usufructuary life interest, which he cannot pass on by will without the family's concurrence.
facts: By his will Y left cocoa farms and buildings to his wife and children. The customary successor sued, saying the properties were family property that Y had taken over as successor to his mother. The trial court accepted this and granted a declaration and an injunction. On appeal, the wife and children argued they could not be sued before probate and that they had a right to live in the house.
held: The appeal was dismissed. A member who makes a farm on family land holds only a life interest; he may alienate that interest but nothing more without the head and principal members, and it reverts to the family on his death, so the devise failed. An executor's title comes from the will, so he can sue and be sued before probate, and so can a beneficiary who meddles with the estate. As the house was family property, not Y's own, the widow and children were licensees only; with no revocation shown, the injunction was discharged.

name: Boateng v Boateng
subject: Land Law
principle: The Akan rule letting children stay in their father's house subject to good behaviour covers only his self-acquired property, not family property he occupied.
facts: A testator left a house to his children by will. The head of his family sued, saying the house was family property. The trial judge found that the land was bought jointly by the testator, his mother, his sister and the plaintiff, and that the house was built by their joint efforts. He declared it family property and gave the family possession. The children appealed on the weight of evidence or, alternatively, for leave to remain.
held: The appeal was dismissed. An appellant who says a judgment is against the weight of evidence must show that from the record. Here the trial judge's findings were well supported by the evidence, so the appellate court would not interfere. The children's customary right to stay in their father's house applies only to his self-acquired property. This was a family house, and since the children were not members of that family they had no interest in it. The family was entitled to immediate possession.

name: Adjowei v Yiadom III
subject: Land Law
principle: In Ashanti, absolute title to stool land may pass by performing the tramma custom without guaha. A sale shown by agreement, demarcation, payment and possession is not undone merely because witnesses were absent.
facts: A syndicate of Shai and Ningo farmers agreed to buy part of Asankare stool land in Ashanti. The land was inspected and demarcated, a custom was performed, the price was paid and the farmers went into possession. Years later the stool began allotting parts of the land to others. The High Court dismissed the syndicate's claim for title, holding that no tramma was given and that any guaha was void because there were no independent witnesses.
held: The appeal was allowed. Guaha is not essential to pass absolute title in Ashanti; tramma, which the evidence showed had been performed, is equally effective. With an agreement, demarcation, payment and possession all proved, it would be unjust to treat the sale as incomplete only because witnesses were absent at the guaha. The only reasonable inference was that the syndicate entered under a completed sale. Sowah JA added, obiter, that part performance could also have helped the purchasers.

name: Tei Angmor & Co v Yiadom III
subject: Land Law
principle: A customary sale of land does not pass ownership unless the guaha ceremony is performed, and an unstamped document relating to transfer of an interest in land is inadmissible.
facts: A group of purchasers claimed title to forest land they said the Nkwatia stool had sold them, though only part of the price had been paid. The Native Court dismissed the claim, but the Land Court found a completed customary sale, relying on an unstamped memorandum that said customary rites had been performed. The stool appealed.
held: The Court of Appeal allowed the stool's appeal. The memorandum was inadmissible because it was unstamped, even though it concerned the transfer of an interest in land. For a customary sale to transfer ownership, guaha must be performed, and there was no evidence that it had been. A later letter from the purchasers' paramount chief, describing them as still negotiating for the land, disproved their claim that the sale had been completed in 1941.

name: Ahmad v Afriyie
subject: Land Law
principle: A customary gift of land is valid and irrevocable when made publicly before witnesses and accepted by the donee through payment of aseda and entry into possession.
facts: The plaintiff, a royal, had served the Keniago stool as an unpaid clerk for nine years. He said the elders, at his request, gave him a stool cocoa farm, that he paid aseda, and that he harvested it for two seasons. A later chief entered the farm and took cocoa, saying the plaintiff had only been a caretaker. The plaintiff sued for title, damages for trespass and an injunction.
held: Apaloo J accepted the plaintiff's account, which an elderly witness to the gift supported. The gift was made in public before witnesses and accepted by payment of aseda and entry into possession. That satisfied the customary requirements for passing title, so the stool had made a valid gift of the farm in 1959, and it could not be revoked.

name: Donkor v Asare
subject: Land Law
principle: A customary sale requires identification of the land, delivery of possession before adjoining owners and guaha on the land; a grant of town land for shared proceeds is like an abusa tenancy, not a licence at will.
facts: At the stool's request, the Oyoko family in possession granted land to the defendants for a football field, with a third of the gate money paid to the family. Later the family purported to sell the land to the plaintiff, with guaha performed at Mamfe rather than on the land, and gave the defendants notice to quit. The plaintiff sued for title and possession and lost in the Native Court.
held: Ollennu J upheld the judgment for the defendants. The plaintiff had not proved the essentials of a customary sale: the parties never agreed on the land sold, it was not delivered to him before the boundary owners, and guaha was not done on the land. The defendants' grant gave them a right in town land similar to an abusa-type tenancy of farmland. That right cannot be ended on short notice unless the tenant denies the grantor's title, so the notice to quit was bad.

name: Norquaye-Tetteh v Malm
subject: Land Law
principle: Economic trees such as mango on stool land are prima facie evidence that a subject or grantee possesses it, so the stool cannot validly grant that land to another.
facts: In 1926 a caretaker of Akumadjaye stool land conveyed a plot to Malm, whose daughters later received it by gift. In 1956 the stool occupant conveyed adjoining plots in the same area to two brothers, who fenced them. Malm's daughter resisted, saying it was her father's land and relying on three mango trees whose fruit the family harvested. The brothers sued for title, damages for trespass and an injunction.
held: Ollennu J dismissed the brothers' claims. Under customary law, economic trees on stool land are prima facie proof of a subject's or grantee's possession, and the stool cannot grant land bearing them. Harvesting the mangoes was strong evidence of the defendants' interest. A grant must also be well publicised locally, with neighbouring owners invited to the demarcation. Neither plaintiff proved the land was vacant when it was conveyed to him.

name: Wuta-Ofei v Danquah
subject: Land Law
principle: To prove possession of vacant, unenclosed land, active use is unnecessary; against a person with no title, the slightest possession with an intention to keep it is enough to sue in trespass.
facts: In 1939 the Osu stool granted the respondent a plot, which was demarcated with pillars marked with her initials and looked after by her mother, but not used. In 1940 an ordinance vested the land in the Chief Secretary. In 1948 the appellant began building on it despite her protests. The West African Court of Appeal refused her a declaration of title but upheld damages for trespass, and he appealed on trespass.
held: The Privy Council dismissed the appeal. The statutory vesting ended her right to possession but did not change the fact of her possession. Possession does not require enclosing or farming the land; what counts as possession depends on the type of land, and vacant land permits little. Against a trespasser with no title, very slight possession is enough. She had never abandoned the possession she took under the 1939 grant and plainly intended to keep it, so she could sue for trespass.
